title: Prodromal Dementia with Lewy Bodies: A Case Series of the 3 Prodromal Types from Clinical Practice
case_prompt:
A 65‐year‐old retired computer repairman and active pilot, with no significant past medical history, reported mild memory problems for one year and thrashing movements during sleep for one year, followed by new‐onset panic attacks over three months. MRI performed after these complaints revealed a fourth ventricular mass, which was resected (pathology: subependymoma). 

Immediately post‐operatively, he became markedly confused with fluctuating attention, initially attributed to post‐operative delirium and benzodiazepine withdrawal. He developed visual hallucinations, poor spatial perception, and a left-leaning gait. During inpatient rehabilitation, cognitive impairment, hallucinations, and new myoclonus persisted despite treatment with aripiprazole, divalproex, donepezil, escitalopram, quetiapine, and clonazepam.

One month after surgery, he was admitted to the neurology service. Examination revealed masked facies, a left‐hand resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, lethargy, perseveration, and halting speech with preserved repetition. He had nearly constant hallucinations and delusions.

Basic laboratory studies were unremarkable. Brain MRI showed post‐surgical changes with meningeal enhancement. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was negative for malignancy. Cerebrospinal fluid studies revealed white blood cells 86 (lymphocytes 46%, monocytes 54%), red blood cells 25, protein 124 mg/dL, glucose 40 mg/dL, findings felt to reflect post‐surgical changes versus inflammation. CSF cultures, RT‐QuIC, and a paraneoplastic autoantibody panel were negative. Electroencephalography demonstrated nonspecific slowing.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Post‐operative delirium was considered because of the immediate confusion attributed to surgery and benzodiazepine withdrawal — “initially attributed to post‐operative delirium and benzodiazepine withdrawal” — but was less likely given the persistence of delirium despite cessation of CNS‐active medications.  
2. Encephalitis was considered because of the prolonged confusion, hallucinations, and inflammatory CSF profile — “for which he received IVIG, though changes were ultimately felt to be post‐surgical rather than inflammatory/infectious” — and was excluded after negative CSF cultures, RT‐QuIC, and paraneoplastic antibody panels.  
3. Prodromal Lewy body dementia was considered due to a history of dream enactment, preoperative memory concerns, new peripheral visual illusions, persistent hallucinations and parkinsonism after delirium resolution, and antipsychotic sensitivity — “While the diagnostic significance of a history of dream enactment in a person with delirium is not yet established, the wife’s report of a 1‐year history of thrashing during nightmares could suggest that this patient had a developing synucleinopathy at his initial presentation… The prolonged delirium was also consistent with delirium‐onset DLB.”
